newsitem.title: UK: Canadian scientists plot toxic mercury rainfall.
newsitem.headline: Canadian scientists plot toxic mercury rainfall.

text.p: A toxic rain of mercury falls on the Arctic every spring just when the Earth's ecosystems are preparing for their first burst of activity of the year, Canadian researchers said in a report published on Thursday.

The researchers at the government research agency Environment Canada, writing in New Scientist magazine, said the reason for the rain of mercury, one of the most poisonous substances known to man, was unclear.

But they said the pattern almost exactly mimics the timing of ozone depletion and suggested that similar processes drive both phenomena. Mercury, alone among heavymetal pollutants, has a boiling point low enough for it to be blown around the world as a gas.
Researcher Bill Schroeder started measuring concentrations of gaseous mercury in the air over Ellsmere Island in northern Canada in the summer of 1994.
Levels remained constant for nine months until late March 1995 when "all hell let loose" and the amount of mercury in the air plummeted, rose and plummeted again many times.
"Bill thought his instruments might be broken so he replaced them and waited a whole year to check the results the next spring. It was the same again," said colleague Leonard Barrie.
One theory is that the gaseous mercury combines with chlorine and bromine to form particles that fall to earth.

Springtime ozone destruction is driven by photochemical reactions involving chlorine and bromine atoms which come from man-made chemicals and from sea salt trapped in the ice-pack and released when the sun returns after the polar winter.
Canadian government scientists are this summer coordinating a nationwide collection of snow by students in a bid to plot the mercury fallout.
